summary: Describes how link-state routing protocols interact with traffic engineering tunnels to create IGP shortcuts. It explains how Dijkstra's shortest path first algorithm can be adapted so routes are calculated over those tunnels.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers can find the best path on a map. This document shows how to add special express lanes to the map.

questions: how do routing protocols use tunnels
subtitle: How routing protocols can use traffic engineering tunnels as express paths.

tldr.problem: Link-state routing protocols like OSPF and IS-IS compute shortest paths using Dijkstra's algorithm, but they don't take advantage of explicitly routed tunnels set up by traffic engineering systems.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC shows how to enhance the SPF algorithm so that routers treat tunnels as potential first hops. During SPF computation, if a tunnel points to a destination node, traffic destined for that node and its children gets routed through the tunnel instead of along regular IP paths.
tldr.outcome: Networks can use traffic engineering tunnels—set up for bandwidth management or redundancy—as dynamic shortcuts chosen by the routing protocol, improving path selection without manual configuration.

facts.label: Loop prevention
facts.value: Tunnel endpoint must be downstream of destination

today: RFC 3906 is an Informational RFC that remains active. IGP shortcuts over MPLS tunnels are used in carrier networks to integrate traffic engineering with dynamic routing, allowing operators to combine the benefits of explicit path control and automatic routing adaptation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Modern networks use two separate systems. Link-state routing (OSPF, IS-IS) computes the shortest path to every destination using Dijkstra's algorithm, a standard algorithm that finds optimal routes based on hop count or link cost. Traffic Engineering creates explicit paths called Label Switched Paths (LSPs) or tunnels through the network, often to reserve bandwidth or bypass congestion.

These two systems were independent: traffic engineering tunnels existed, but Dijkstra's algorithm didn't consider them. Operators had to manually configure static routes to push traffic into tunnels. This RFC solves that by making the routing algorithm tunnel-aware.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers normally follow shortest paths. Tunnels are special express routes. This shows how routers can automatically pick tunnel routes when they make sense.

sections.title: Enhanced Shortest Path First Algorithm
sections.content:
The key insight is simple: during SPF computation, when a router discovers the shortest path to a destination node, it has three choices for the first hop:

Option 1: If a tunnel points directly to this node, use the tunnel as the first hop.

Option 2: If the node is directly connected via a physical link, use that link.

Option 3: If neither applies, copy the first-hop information from parent nodes in the shortest-path tree.

The result is that traffic destined for a tunnel's endpoint flows over the tunnel. More importantly, traffic destined for nodes beyond the tunnel endpoint also flows over the tunnel, because the downstream nodes inherit the tunnel as their first hop from their parent.

For example, if a tunnel reaches router C, and router D is only reachable via C, traffic to D automatically uses the tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm asks: is there a tunnel to this destination? If yes, use it. If not, use the normal path. Destinations beyond the tunnel endpoint also use the tunnel.

sections.title: Handling Complex Topologies
sections.content:
When multiple equal-cost paths exist, the algorithm handles them correctly. For instance, if traffic can reach a destination via both a tunnel and a native IP path with the same cost, the router can choose either or both (load-sharing).

The RFC gives a detailed example: in a network where a tunnel reaches an intermediate node but multiple paths continue beyond it, traffic to destinations beyond that point can load-balance across the tunnel and other paths if they have equal cost.

A critical safety rule ensures the algorithm is loop-free: a router should only route a packet into a tunnel if the tunnel's endpoint is closer to the packet's destination than the tunnel's starting point. The algorithm enforces this automatically because tunnels are already set up and the SPF computation respects the topology.
sections.plainLanguage: If two routes to the same place cost the same, the router can split traffic between them. The algorithm avoids loops by making sure the tunnel gets closer to the destination.

sections.title: Tuning Tunnel Preferences with Metrics
sections.content:
Sometimes operators want to prefer tunnels over native paths or vice versa, even when costs are equal. The RFC describes two approaches.

Absolute (fixed) metric: Assign a fixed cost to all traffic through a tunnel, independent of the underlying network topology. For example, always cost 5. This is simple but inflexible—all destinations through the tunnel get the same cost regardless of how far away they are.

Relative (dynamic) metric: Adjust the computed SPF cost by a fixed amount—positive to make the tunnel less attractive, negative to make it more attractive, or zero for no adjustment (the default). For example, subtract 5 from the computed cost to prefer the tunnel.

The RFC provides a concrete example: if the native path to a destination costs 20 hops, and a tunnel has a relative metric of -5, the tunnel route is installed at cost 15, making it preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: You can tell the router to prefer or avoid tunnels by adjusting their cost, making certain tunnels more or less attractive for traffic.

sections.title: Security Impact
sections.content: This RFC does not introduce new security weaknesses in OSPF or IS-IS. The security properties of the underlying routing protocols remain unchanged. However, because traffic is now influenced by both routing and traffic engineering decisions, operators must understand the interaction: a poorly configured tunnel or metric could inadvertently shift traffic in ways that violate security policies.
sections.plainLanguage: The routing protocol is still as secure as before, but operators need to think about where traffic actually goes through tunnels.
